title: I just want to grow and follow Jesus well
seoTitle: How to Grow in Your Faith: Habits, Grace, and a Rule of Life
description: Want to grow in your faith but feel stuck? How growth in Christ really happens: ordinary practices, other people, a rule of life you can keep, and grace.
summary: How faith actually grows: ordinary practices, other people, a rule small enough to keep, and grace for the dry seasons.
askedAs: how to grow closer to God
how to be a better Christian
answer: You want to grow. Nothing is falling apart, but you'd like to know God better, to pray and read the Bible with some steadiness, and to be kinder and more patient a year from now. Maybe you've started reading plans and dropped them by February, or you've followed Jesus for years and feel stuck. Growth in Christ is God's work in you before it's yours. It comes slowly, through ordinary things like Scripture, prayer, worship, and friendship, and you're invited to take part in it, not to produce it. Tonight, read [Psalm 1](/study/bible/psalms/1) slowly and pray one line of it back to God. Then choose one small practice for this week, and tell someone you're trying.
happening:
When people say *I want to grow*, they usually mean several things at once. You want to know God, not only know about him. You'd like to pray without drifting, open the Bible without feeling lost, and stop repeating the same failures: the short temper at the end of the day, the scrolling that eats the evening, the flash of envy when a friend does well. Underneath, there's often a quiet worry that other Christians are further along. You may have bought the journal and started the plan, only to find it slipping by the third week. If you've been a Christian for years, you may struggle to name what has changed, and conclude that something is wrong with you.

The common explanations each hold some truth. The practical one says you need better habits and a system to keep them, and that's right as far as it goes: we're shaped by what we repeat, and the church knew it long before the productivity books did. But habits can be kept for any reason, and a perfect streak of morning devotions can sit beside a cold heart. A system can tell you how to repeat something. It can't tell you what to love, or who is doing the changing.

The religious explanations pull against each other. One says try harder, and lets guilt do the pushing. The other says stop trying and trust, since growth is God's business. Each has hold of something. Effort matters, though guilt makes a poor engine for it. And the growth really is God's, but that doesn't leave you with nothing to do. The New Testament is full of effort, telling believers to “train yourself for godliness” (1 Timothy 4:7) and to “make every effort” (2 Peter 1:5), and it's just as clear that God gives the growth. Hold only one half and you'll end up exhausted or adrift.

Then there's the explanation from feeling: you're growing when you feel close to God. Sometimes you will, and that's a gift. But feelings rise and fall with sleep, grief, and the seasons of a life, and some of the deepest growth happens when God feels far away.

What these leave out is that Christian growth isn't self-improvement with God as your coach. It's being made like Christ. God does it through ordinary means, among other people, over a long time, and he gives you a real part in it. Its measure is love.

Sometimes *stuck* is something else. If you've lost interest in nearly everything, not only prayer, or a heaviness won't lift, talk with a doctor as well as a pastor.

scripture.intro: Scripture doesn't hand you a program for growing. It gives pictures: a tree planted by water, a vine and its branches, a harvest of character, a church dressing itself in compassion. Read them slowly, and notice how much of the growing is God's doing, how much is asked of you, and how rarely anyone grows alone.

passages.text: Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, or set foot on the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of mockers. But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night. He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither, and who prospers in all he does. Not so the wicked! For they are like chaff driven off by the wind. Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous. For the LORD guards the path of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.
passages.reading: Psalm 1 opens the book of Psalms with two ways a life can go. Notice the slow slide in its first verse: walking in the counsel of the wicked, then setting foot on the path of sinners, then sitting down among the mockers. We're being formed by something, usually a little at a time. The psalm's answer is delight, a person returning to God's instruction “day and night” (verse 2). The tree didn't plant itself; it was “planted by streams of water” (verse 3), and it bears fruit in season, not every week of the year. Its prospering isn't a promise of an easy life, either: two psalms later, the book is already crying to God about enemies (3:1). If your growth feels slow, the psalm isn't surprised. Trees are slow. Unlike chaff, they're also hard to blow away.

passages.text: “I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard. He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful. You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you. Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me. I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.
passages.reading: Jesus said this on the night he was arrested, after Judas had gone out (13:30), to eleven men who would scatter within hours (16:32). He tells them they're already clean because of his word (verse 3) before he asks anything of them. His command is one word, repeated: remain. Branches don't strain to make grapes; they stay joined to the vine, which is why he can say “apart from Me you can do nothing” (verse 5). Remaining isn't passive; a few lines on, he ties it to keeping his commandments (verse 10). The Father prunes branches that already bear fruit (verse 2), though not every loss is pruning. Just past these lines, verse 6 says a branch that doesn't remain is thrown away and burned, and Christians disagree in good faith about what that means for a believer. Some read it as describing people who were near Jesus without being joined to him, and rest on his promise that no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand (10:28). Others read it, with Hebrews 3:12, as a warning that a believer can turn away, and take comfort that it's aimed at turning away, not at weakness. Either way, he said these things to men about to fail him, and after the resurrection he came back to them (20:19).

passages.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit.
passages.reading: Paul wrote Galatians to churches being told that faith in Christ wasn't enough without circumcision and the law, a burden he called “a yoke of slavery” (5:1). In the same chapter he warns against the opposite ditch, using freedom “as an opportunity for the flesh” (5:13). The acts of the flesh are a heap of things we produce (5:19-21); the fruit of the Spirit is one harvest. The list leaves out hours logged in prayer, knowledge, and visible ministry. It names character, much of which, like patience and kindness, can only be tested among people. And it ends with a walk: “let us walk in step with the Spirit” (verse 25). He sets the pace.

passages.text: Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity. Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were called as members of one body. And be thankful. Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God. And whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him.
passages.reading: The letter to the Colossians was written to a church being offered a more impressive spirituality: visions, and strict rules of self-denial that are “of no value against the indulgence of the flesh” (2:23). Anyone writing a rule of life should hear that warning: practices help when they keep you near Christ and his people, and they go sour when they become a way to impress God or anyone else. The letter's counsel is to hold fast to Christ, from whom the whole body “grows as God causes it to grow” (2:19), and then to get dressed. They're called “holy and beloved” (verse 12) before they're told what to wear, and none of these clothes can be worn alone in a room. Even Scripture and song are shared (verse 16). Then it widens: “whatever you do, in word or deed” (verse 17). Growth reaches the kitchen, the commute, and the inbox.

whyHard:
If growing is good, and God is the one who grows us, why is it so hard to keep at? Busyness is part of it, but people with time to spare get stuck too, and so many sincere efforts end in guilt.

Part of the trouble is an old American picture of growth. In his autobiography, Benjamin Franklin describes a project he set himself, to arrive at moral perfection. He listed thirteen virtues, kept a little book with a column for each day, and marked his failures with black spots. He never got there, though he believed the attempt made him a better and happier man, and a skeptic is right that habits like his change people, God or no God. I came to faith from atheism, and I won't pretend the skeptic is wrong about that. But look at what happened with humility. He added it to his list after a friend told him he was thought proud, admitted he gained more of its appearance than its reality, and guessed that if he ever conquered his pride, he would be proud of his humility. He had found where self-improvement runs out: at the self doing the improving.

Without noticing, many of us carried Franklin's chart into church. Spiritual growth became self-improvement with Bible verses: a streak to protect, a reading plan that works like a performance review. When it goes well we're quietly proud, when it slips we're ashamed, and either way it's about us. As the philosopher James K. A. Smith has argued, we're shaped less by what we think than by what we love, and our loves are trained by what we repeatedly do. So the rest of the week is forming us too, and a few minutes with the Bible won't outweigh it by willpower.

Pastors like me have to own our part. We've often measured growth by what was easy to count, attendance and activity, or treated it as a moment, the decision or the retreat, with little to offer for the long stretch afterward. People learned from us that growth happens in a spiritual compartment, while the job, the money, the body, and the marriage sit outside it. And sometimes we've preached grace to bring people in, then handed them a treadmill.

The older picture of growth was slow, shared, and woven through ordinary life. The first believers devoted themselves to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer (Acts 2:42). In the sixth century Benedict of Nursia wrote a short rule for a community of monks. In its opening he calls the life he is setting up a school for the Lord's service and hopes to set down nothing harsh or burdensome, and in its last chapter he calls it a little rule for beginners. It assumed that growth would take a lifetime, and company.

Beneath all of it lies an old confusion about grace. When growth stalls, we swing between a treadmill that treats God's love as a wage and a shrug that leaves everything to God. Both can pass for faith. The first turns God into an employer, and the second into a caretaker who asks nothing of us. Paul, writing in chains to a church he loved, held the two halves in one breath: “continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act” (Philippians 2:12-13). Dallas Willard drew the distinction simply: grace is opposed to earning, not to effort. You can't earn what has been given. You can work hard at staying near the one who gives it.

So if you've been treating your growth as Franklin's chart with a cross on the cover, no wonder it wore you out. Fruit can't be manufactured, and you were never asked to manufacture it. You were asked to remain.

thisWeek.intro: Don't try all of these. Pick one or two that fit your week, small enough to keep on a bad day. You'll grow more from what you return to than from what you start.

steps.title: Read one psalm a day
steps.body: Start with Psalm 1 and read one psalm a day, slowly, aloud if you can. When a line is true for you, pray it back to God in your own words; when it isn't, pray it for someone it fits. For a set course, print [The Psalms in Thirty Days](/plans#psalms-in-30-days). If you miss a day, don't make it up. Just read today's.

steps.title: Take an honest look
steps.body: You can't tend what you won't look at. [The Whole-Life Assessment](/life/assessment) takes about eight minutes: thirty statements on the inner life, the body, the home, work and money, and the wider world. Nothing leaves your browser, and it hands back a simple rule for the season. The [Life Audit](/tools/life-audit) covers eight areas of life. Pray first: “Search me, O God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23). Neither is a grade; your lowest areas are simply where to begin.

steps.title: Be with your church on Sunday
steps.body: Go this Sunday. Listen for the Word, sing even when you don't feel like it, and receive the Lord's Supper when your church offers it (many churches ask that you be baptized first). Then stay a few minutes afterward, because the people are part of how God grows you. No church yet? Pick one to visit and choose the Sunday now. If church is where you were hurt, read [The church hurt me](/help/church-hurt) first; you don't have to walk back in alone.

steps.title: Keep a few hours of rest
steps.body: Choose a stretch of hours this week, half a day if a whole one isn't possible, and stop: no work, no errands, no catching up. Worship, eat a long meal, walk, nap, call a friend. Whatever you believe about how the Sabbath command applies to Christians, Jesus was plain about whom it serves: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). If that's impossible right now, start with an hour.

steps.title: Ask one person to walk with you
steps.body: Ask someone you trust who is a little further along (a friend, an older Christian, your pastor) to meet once a month and ask how you're really doing. Read the same passage between visits. In time, tell them where you struggle; the letter of James tells believers to “confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed” (5:16).

steps.title: Do one kindness no one will see
steps.body: Love of neighbor is where growth shows, so practice it where no one will applaud. Do one hidden thing for someone this week: a meal, an errand, a note, an hour with someone lonely. Don't post it or mention it. Jesus told his followers to give in secret, because the Father “sees what is done in secret” (Matthew 6:4). Quiet service trains the heart away from performance.

steps.title: Write a rule small enough to keep
steps.body: At the end of the week, write on one card the two or three practices that helped, with when and where you'll keep them: a psalm before breakfast, church on Sunday, coffee with a friend once a month. That's a rule of life, a trellis that can't make anything grow but gives a growing life something to climb. [The Rule of Life Builder](/tools/rule-of-life) can help. Show the card to one person, and revisit it when the season changes.

moreHelp.body:
Wanting to grow is a pastoral matter, and the right first call is usually a pastor or an older Christian you trust. But if you've lost interest in nearly everything, not only prayer and church, if your sleep or appetite has changed, or you feel hopeless or worthless, and it has lasted two weeks or more, see a doctor or a licensed counselor too. Do the same if faith has become a place of fear: if you're sure God will punish you unless your devotions are perfect, or you confess the same sin again and again and never feel forgiven. Needing that help is no mark against your faith. If a church or leader uses talk of growth to control what you read, whom you see, or what you give, that is spiritual abuse; talk with someone outside the group, and read [The church hurt me](/help/church-hurt). If someone at home threatens or hurts you, or uses God to frighten and control you, your safety comes first: call 911 if you're in danger, and use the help lines at the end of this page.

To find a counselor, ask your doctor for a referral, check your insurer's directory, or ask a pastor which counselors nearby they trust. If you want a Christian counselor, say so. Christian or not, make sure they're licensed in your state; your state's licensing board can confirm it.
signs: You have thoughts of ending your life or of not wanting to be alive. Call or text 988 now, or 911 if you are in danger.
Prayer, church, and nearly everything else have gone flat, with changes in sleep or appetite, for two weeks or more.
Fear of failing God takes hours of your day, or you never feel forgiven however often you confess.
Fasting or another discipline has become a way to punish yourself or to control your weight.
A church, group, or leader uses talk of growth to control what you read, whom you see, or what you give.
Someone at home threatens or hurts you, or uses God to frighten and control you.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need the right words. To a pastor: *I want to grow, and I don't know where to start. Could we meet a few times?* To a doctor or counselor: *Prayer, church, and almost everything else have gone flat for about a month, and I'm not sleeping well.* Say how long it has been. If your faith matters to you, say so: *I'm a Christian, and I'd like a counselor who respects that.*
moreHelp.cost: Meeting with a pastor or a friend costs nothing, and neither do most of the practices on this page. Counseling fees vary, so ask about sliding-scale fees, look for a community mental health center or a university training clinic, and check whether your employer offers an employee assistance program, which often covers a few sessions. Some churches keep a benevolence fund for counseling, and it's fine to ask.

helping.body: Maybe your teenager asked how to read the Bible, a newer Christian asked you to disciple them, or someone in your group says they feel stuck. The most useful thing you can give is your company. Read the same passage and talk about it. Pray together, briefly and plainly. Let them see your ordinary practices, including the days you miss. Paul could tell the Corinthians, “You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1), and much of faith is still learned by watching. I'm the father of five sons, and I'm convinced they learn more from what I repeat than from anything I tell them. Don't just hand them a program, and don't grade their quiet times; ask about love, patience, and honesty, because that's what growth looks like. Tell them about your own dry seasons, so theirs don't frighten them. With a child, keep it short, steady, and warm, and welcome every question. If you lead a church or a group, measure whether people are becoming more loving, not only more active.
say: Want to read the same psalm this week and talk about it Friday?
Missing a day doesn't undo anything. Just pick it back up.
What would you like God to grow in you this year?
Growth is slow, and you're not behind.
dontSay: You should be further along by now.
Real Christians have a quiet time every day.
Just let go and let God.
If you loved God, you'd want to read your Bible.
Don't worry about it. You're fine.
helping.next: Offer to walk [Eight Weeks Toward One Undivided Life](/plans/whole-life) together, or work through [Spiritual Habits: A Bible Study on Formation](/studyguides/habits-and-formation) with a few friends. Set a time to check in, and keep it. Pray for them by name. If you notice the signs above, help them call a doctor or counselor, and offer to sit with them while they do. If they say they've thought about not wanting to be alive, ask them plainly whether they're thinking about suicide, and stay with them while they call or text 988. If they're afraid of someone at home, ask how it's safe to reach them, and point them to the help lines at the end of this page.

prayer:
Father, I want to grow, and I'm tired of starting over. I've made plans and broken them. I've measured myself against people who seem further along, and mistaken being busy for being close to you.

Your Son said that apart from him I can do nothing. I believe it on my good days. Teach me to remain in him on the ordinary ones: before the phone in the morning, at the table, in traffic, in the conversation I'd rather avoid.

Plant me by the water. Grow in me what I can't manufacture: love, patience, a little more gentleness than last year. When something in me needs cutting back, help me trust your hands. When the season is dry, keep me at the well, and send someone to walk with me.

You began a good work in me. I'm trusting you to finish it, in your time and not mine. In Jesus' name, amen.

faq.q: How do I grow in my faith?
faq.a: Mostly through ordinary things, kept up over time, with other people. The first Christians devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer (Acts 2:42), and those are still the heart of it, along with rest, service, and friendship. Christians often call these the spiritual disciplines or the means of grace. None of them makes you grow by itself. Paul said of his work in Corinth, “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Start with one practice you can keep, and give it months, not days.

faq.q: What is a rule of life?
faq.a: A rule of life is a short, written pattern of practices you mean to keep, fitted to your actual week: when you'll pray and read Scripture, where you'll worship, how you'll rest, whom you'll meet with, and how you'll serve. The idea comes from the old monastic rules, written so a community could live and pray together, and many Christians now keep a simple personal version. A good rule works like a trellis, holding a growing life up toward the light. Keep yours small enough for your worst week. [The Rule of Life Builder](/tools/rule-of-life) will help you write one.

faq.q: Why do I feel stuck spiritually?
faq.a: Different things can feel the same from the inside. It may be a dry season, when God feels far away though you're doing what you know to do. That isn't failure, and the Psalms give words for it: “My soul thirsts for God, the living God” (Psalm 42:2). Keep the practices, and tell God honestly how they feel. It may be a sin you've stopped fighting or a wound you haven't faced, which an honest friend can help you see. Growth can also be too slow to see from the inside, the way parents rarely notice a child growing until last year's coat won't button. And exhaustion or depression can feel like being stuck; if a heaviness won't lift, see a doctor.

faq.q: Isn't trying hard to grow just trying to earn God's love?
faq.a: It can turn into that, and then it's exhausting. But effort and earning aren't the same thing. Earning tries to put God in your debt; effort means taking part in what he's already doing. The second letter of Peter holds both together: God's “divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness” (2 Peter 1:3), and “for this very reason, make every effort” to add to faith a ladder of qualities that ends in love (1:5-7). If missing a morning leaves you sure God is angry, that's the treadmill talking. The cure is to hear the gospel again, not to try harder.

faq.q: How do I know if I'm actually growing?
faq.a: Not mainly by how you feel, how much you know, or how busy you are at church. Scripture points instead to the fruit of the Spirit: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23). In ordinary life that often looks like noticing your sin sooner and confessing it faster, forgiving more quickly, caring less about seeming spiritual, and loving people you used to avoid. Jesus said all the Law and the Prophets hang on love for God and love for neighbor (Matthew 22:37-40). You may be the last to see your own growth, so ask someone who knows you well.

slots.note: The page says only that James came to faith from atheism and will not pretend that habits fail to change people without God. He could add, in his own words, what growth looked like in his first years as a Christian and what he wishes someone had told him then. The section stands without it.

Where James lands on eternal security, the question John 15:6 raises: whether a true believer can finally fall away. The John 15 reading names verse 6 instead of hiding it, states both readings in good faith, each with a verse (John 10:28; Hebrews 3:12) and its comfort, and does not land; the creeds do not settle it. If he wants a landing, it should be in his own words, in one place.
James could describe the rule of life he actually keeps as a pastor, as one real example beside step seven. Nothing has been written for him.

Step four says only that Christians differ on how the Sabbath command applies now, and takes no side. If James wants to say where he lands, it should be in his own words, in one place; the step stands without it.

The section states only James's conviction, as a father of five sons, that children learn more from what a parent repeats than from what he tells them. James was raised without a father; he could add, in his own words, who showed him how to follow Jesus when there was no father at home to imitate, and how he tries to form his sons through ordinary repetition. The section rests on 1 Corinthians 11:1 and stands without it; no story has been written for him.

sources.claim: Benjamin Franklin's autobiography describes his project of arriving at moral perfection: thirteen virtues, a little book with a column for each day, failures marked with black spots. He added humility after a Quaker friend told him he was generally thought proud, admitted he had little success with the reality of humility but a good deal with its appearance, remarked that even if he could conceive he had completely overcome his pride he would probably be proud of his humility, and judged that the attempt made him a better and happier man than he would otherwise have been. The page paraphrases and does not quote.
sources.cite: Benjamin Franklin, The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Part Two (Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection), Standard Ebooks text, chapter IX

sources.claim: James K. A. Smith argues that human beings are shaped less by what they think than by what they love, and that their loves are trained by repeated practices (liturgies), including the practices of ordinary secular life.
sources.cite: James K. A. Smith, You Are What You Love: The Spiritual Power of Habit (Brazos Press, 2016), a popular version of Desiring the Kingdom (Baker Academic, 2009); Internet Archive catalog record

sources.claim: Benedict's Rule, written for monks in the sixth century, says in its Prologue that it will establish a school for the service of the Lord and hopes to introduce nothing harsh or burdensome, and in its last chapter (73) calls itself a little rule written for beginners. The page paraphrases and does not quote.
sources.cite: The Rule of Saint Benedict, Prologue and chapter 73, translated by Leonard J. Doyle as St. Benedict's Rule for Monasteries (Project Gutenberg)

sources.claim: Dallas Willard taught that grace is not opposed to effort but to earning. The page names the thinker and the idea in its own words and names no book.
sources.cite: Dallas Willard. The line is often cited to The Great Omission (HarperSanFrancisco, 2006); that attribution could not be confirmed here, so it is not made on the page.

sources.claim: Depression symptoms are present most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, and include loss of interest or pleasure and changes in sleep and appetite.
sources.cite: National Institute of Mental Health, Depression

reviewed.notes: Second pass (editor), 2026-10-01, over the writer's draft; supersedes the writer's self-check. Validator clean (node scripts/validate-needs.mjs whole-life, 4,477 words) and the CarePage render test passes. Truth: every Scripture setting re-read with scripts/bsb.mjs --verses (Psalm 1, 3:1, 42:1-3, 80:8, 139:23; John 10:27-29, 13:10-11, 13:30, 15:1-12, 16:32, 20:19, 21:15-17; Galatians 5:1-4, 5:13, 5:19-25; Colossians 1:1-2, 2:18-23, 3:12-17; Philippians 1:7, 1:13, 2:12-13; Hebrews 3:12-14; Acts 2:42; 1 Timothy 4:7-8; 2 Peter 1:3-8; Mark 2:23-28; James 5:16; Matthew 6:1-4, 22:37-40; 1 Corinthians 3:5-7, 11:1). Direct fetches and web search were both unavailable in this pass, so outside claims stay only where they are well-established knowledge the editor is certain of: Franklin's project of moral perfection in Part Two of the Autobiography (thirteen virtues, the little book, the black spots, humility added after a friend said he was thought proud, more its appearance than its reality, proud of his humility, a better and happier man); James K. A. Smith's thesis that we are shaped by what we love and our loves by what we repeatedly do (the prose names no book); the Prologue of Benedict's Rule (a school for the Lord's service, nothing harsh or burdensome) and its last chapter (a little rule for beginners, added here); Willard's distinction between earning and effort, now credited to Willard with no book, because the writer's attribution to The Great Omission could not be confirmed (the sources entry says so and points to dwillard.org); NIMH's two-week course for depression symptoms. No source URL was opened; re-open each before release.
